race.office: Governor of Alaska (open seat; Gov. Mike Dunleavy term-limited)

nominee.t: Advanced after the primary (5th place) when Begich and Bishop withdrew. Aug. 18, 2026 top-four nonpartisan primary (17 candidates, 164,303 votes): Kreiss-Tomkins 37,006 (22.5%); Begich 34,172 (20.8%, withdrew); Wilson 16,468 (10.0%); Bronson 13,364 (8.1%); Taylor 11,928 (7.3%); Bishop 11,527 (7.0%, withdrew). Running mate: businesswoman Candice ('Candi') English.

ballot.t: Four-candidate ranked-choice general ballot (Nov. 3, 2026): Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D) / Zac Johnson; Bernadette Wilson (R) / Mike Shower; Dave Bronson (R) / Josh Church; Treg Taylor (R) / Candice English. Tom Begich (D, 2nd) withdrew Aug. 28 and endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins; Click Bishop (R, 6th) also withdrew, which let Taylor (5th) advance. The Division of Elections' candidate list was updated after 11 p.m. Sept. 4 to show Taylor with English as running mate. First general ballots mailed starting Sept. 18.

certification.t: Disqualified, then reinstated. (1) APOC voted 4–1 in late August to recommend that Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom not certify him. He had reported more than $1M in rental income but listed tenants only by first name and last initial (July 27 list), after an earlier APOC order and a July 21, 2026 notice of deficiency; the 30-day amendment window had passed. (2) On Mon., Aug. 31, Dahlstrom said she would not certify him. His running mate, Candice English, could take the top spot on the ticket if she named a running mate by 5 p.m. that day; she named Taylor's wife, Jodi Taylor. If English had been removed instead, Click Bishop was next in line. (3) On Fri., Sept. 4, after 10 p.m., Dahlstrom reversed herself and certified Taylor, along with state House candidate Jose Tagle. She cited an unpublished, 'informal' and 'preliminary' review by the Department of Law, which Taylor had led until August 2025. The review found 'numerous potential discrepancies' across many candidates' disclosures, and she wrote that she could not apply APOC's recommendations 'with confidence across the field.' APOC had not withdrawn its recommendation and did not hold the special meeting she expected. (4) After 11 p.m. Sept. 4, the Division of Elections list showed Taylor for governor with English as running mate, so the Jodi Taylor ticket no longer appears. No lawsuit over either decision was reported as of Sept. 5.

oneliner.t: Republican former Alaska attorney general (acting from Jan. 30, 2021, confirmed May 11, 2021, resigned Aug. 29, 2025) and Anchorage real-estate co-owner, reinstated to the governor's ballot on Sept. 4, 2026 after a four-day disqualification over his financial disclosure.

born.t: May 19, 1976 (Wikipedia; his pamphlet gives age 50). Birthplace not found.

upbringing.t: His own statement says he was raised by a single mother and worked nights to pay for school; no independent record of this was found. He briefly attended the U.S. Air Force Academy, though Wikipedia flags this as needing a citation. He then earned a B.A. in political science (2001) and a J.D. (2004) at Brigham Young University. He reports 27 years in Alaska. He and his wife Jodi have six children.

education.deg: None — attended U.S. Air Force Academy (briefly)

education.school: BYU J. Reuben Clark Law School

career.role: Attorney General (acting Jan. 30, 2021; confirmed May 11, 2021; resigned Aug. 29, 2025)
Co-owner, real estate restoration/development (with his wife, bought a downtown Anchorage apartment building in 2023 while AG)

platform.t: Cut waste, balance the budget and protect the PFD. Says he is 'completely against' any new tax: on families, sales, industries or corporations.

Supports vouchers and a constitutional amendment letting funding follow the child to private schools. Stop 'woke indoctrination' in schools. As AG he defended the state's correspondence-school allotment program, still in court.
Expand resource extraction to keep working-age Alaskans; 'partner with President Trump'. Says data centers are a reality and Alaska can learn from other states.
Opposes HB 78 (defined-benefit pensions) and the 2024 voter-approved minimum-wage/paid-sick-leave law, calling the latter government overreach.
Protect girls' sports; stop trawling that damages the environment.

promises.t: Balance the budget and protect the PFD.
Seek a constitutional amendment letting education funding follow the child.

claims.claim: Third longest-serving Alaska attorney general in state history.

said.where: Official Election Pamphlet candidate statement (stand-in for campaign bio page)

record.t: His own Department of Law said the same in its Aug. 21, 2025 resignation release. He served about four years seven months (Jan. 30, 2021–Aug. 29, 2025). An independent list of AG tenures could not be retrieved (Wikipedia's table was empty).

claims.claim: As a prosecutor, helped drive crime to a 40-year low.

record.t: KTUU (July 2025) linked DPS 'Crime in Alaska 2023' and the Criminal Justice Data Analysis Commission's 2024 report as support for the declining-crime claim. Arrests and citations fell from 30,810 (2015) to 21,648 (2023), and his department reported violent crime down nearly 5% in 2023. The decline began before he became AG, and how much is owed to his office is his own characterization. The 40-year comparison itself was not checked.

His department's 2025 release says sexual assault fell 'more than 25 percent since 2018'. KTUU reported about 20% since 2018 and 15.7% in the latest year. The baseline (2018) predates his time as AG (2021); he was deputy AG for the civil division from 2018. In July 2025 he said he was 'a little wary' of the numbers because reporting may have fallen.

claims.claim: Helped pass a law raising the charge to second-degree murder for dealers whose drugs cause a death.

record.t: HB 66, signed by Gov. Dunleavy in July 2024, makes distributing or manufacturing drugs that cause a fatal overdose second-degree murder. AG Taylor spoke at the signing, and his department's 2025 release credits it with advancing reforms to hold dealers accountable for overdose deaths. His personal role in drafting or passage is not detailed in the sources opened.

claims.claim: Raised by a single mother; worked nights to put himself through school.

record.t: No independent biographical record was found.

claims.claim: "The Ninth Circuit struck down Alaska's unconstitutional contribution limits years ago" (defending his post-deadline self-funding).

said.where: Campaign manager Evan Lee, statement to Alaska Beacon

record.t: The 2021 Ninth Circuit ruling struck down limits on donations from people other than the candidate. It did not address AS 15.13.078's cap on candidates funding their own campaigns after July 17. APOC's 2021 order also treated Thompson v. Hebdon as being about individual contribution limits. No court has ruled on the self-funding cap, and court records showed no suit by Taylor challenging it.

claims.claim: Says he complied with state financial-disclosure requirements (withholding tenants' last names to protect privacy).

said.where: Public statements reported by ADN/Juneau Independent

record.t: This is an unresolved legal dispute. APOC staff and commissioners (4–1) found his initials-only tenant list did not substantially comply with AS 39.50.030. Taylor argues the statute does not require each source's 'full name'. The lieutenant governor certified him anyway after a Department of Law review that questioned APOC's even-handedness. No court has ruled.

said.t: Called reversing Alaska's ranking as the state with the highest sex-crime rate his first priority. Backed a budget request for 10 new prosecutors and nine support staff focused on sex crimes.

did.t: Reported sexual-assault cases fell about 20% since 2018. His department says thousands of backlogged sexual-assault kits were cleared. He cautioned the drop might partly reflect less reporting. Whether the 10 prosecutor positions were funded and filled was not checked.

said.t: His campaign called the post-July 17 self-funding cap unconstitutional.

did.t: Gave $300,000 in cash after the deadline ($260,000 on Aug. 3 plus $40,000) without filing any court challenge to the law.

saydo.note: Context only; the post-deadline money is rated once, in the claims check.

promises_prev.promise: As AG: make reversing Alaska's top-in-the-nation sex-crime rate the first priority (10 new sex-crime prosecutors requested)

evidence.t: His department and KTUU reported that sexual assault fell 20% to more than 25% from 2018 through 2024, and that thousands of backlogged kits were cleared.

complicating.t: Taylor himself questioned whether the drop reflects less reporting. Alaska's national ranking after his tenure was not retrieved, and the prosecutor-hiring outcome was not checked.

promises_prev.promise: As AG: no blanket ethics waivers, unlike past administrations

evidence.t: He made the pledge at his 2021 confirmation hearing. No record of waivers issued during his tenure was found.

complicating.t: Not checkable with sources reached; listed as unscored.

promises_prev.promise: As AG: avoid a repeat of the prior string of legal losses

evidence.t: His department says it joined or led more than 80 suits against federal actions, defended the Willow project and challenged vaccine and mask mandates. It gives no case names or win/loss record.

complicating.t: No independent tally of case outcomes was retrieved; the correspondence-allotment defense is still in court.

entries.t: As AG, supported the Pebble proposal and opposed the federal veto that blocked it.
As AG, defended the correspondence-school allotment program.
Vouchers plus a constitutional amendment so funding follows the child.
While APOC was moving against him, urged Wilson and Bronson to form one ticket and said he would endorse it, without saying he would withdraw.
After reinstatement, stayed in and, with Bronson, urged conservatives to rank all Republicans.

About $1M by the July pre-primary report (under $150K of it since February), and more than $1.58M by the Aug. 18 pre-primary filing. Post-primary (Oct. 5) totals were not found.

money_history.office: Governor (as reported by Alaska Beacon from the pre-primary filing)

note.t: He reported more than $1 million in rental income from a downtown Anchorage apartment building he and his wife bought in 2023, while he was AG. In Sept. 2025 APOC ordered him to amend his report and file the tenant list electronically. His June 1, 2026 annual report again lacked it, and APOC issued a notice of deficiency on July 21. Wikipedia reports his wife's own filings also omitted tenant names; that is her record, not his. He offered to give APOC the names privately, saying tenants had been harassed.

revolving.t: Before state service he was senior counsel at ASRC Energy Services (an oil-field services subsidiary of a Native regional corporation) and counsel at McKinley Capital Management (dates not given). He resigned as AG on Aug. 29, 2025 and announced for governor Sept. 16, 2025. In Sept. 2026 the department he had led produced the review the lieutenant governor cited in reinstating him.

democracy.t: After his reinstatement: 'Alaskans should decide our elections. Not political insiders. Not special interests. Not the establishment.' He said opponents had tried to remove him and reversed only because the same standard would have removed several candidates.
No statement by Taylor on the 2020 or 2024 presidential results was found in sources searched. His role as AG in election-related litigation was not reviewed.

debates.note: Participated: Last Frontier Republican Club forum (Sept. 8) and Dena'ina Center forum (Sept. 21). Not listed at the Aug. 26 AOGA forum, which preceded his advancement. No declined debate found.

note.t: Self-reported 27 years in Alaska, all in Anchorage.

checks.legal: CourtListener was blocked. Alaska CourtView was not searched directly. Searched news (ADN, Alaska Beacon, Alaska Public Media, Juneau Independent, KTUU) and Wikipedia for lawsuits, ethics complaints and APOC actions. Found the APOC tenant-disclosure matter (2025 order, 2026 recommendation, disqualification and reinstatement) and the self-funding-limit issue. No lawsuit or criminal matter found; the Beacon noted no state or federal suit by Taylor over the self-funding cap.
checks.foreign: FARA was blocked. No foreign ties found in news or his pamphlet. McKinley Capital Management's client base was not reviewed.
checks.claims: Campaign site tregforak.com could not be fetched (tool provenance block). As a stand-in, used his candidate-authored Official Election Pamphlet statement (all bio claims) plus two campaign statements on the APOC disputes. No ad scripts were found. Seven claims: 4 rated (unverifiable excluded): 1 true, 2 partly, 1 misleading; 3 unverifiable.
checks.democracy: Never in Congress. Searched news and Wikipedia for statements on 2020/2024 presidential results; none found. AG-era election litigation not reviewed.

legal.t: One tenant-name disclosure dispute at two stages. In Sept. 2025 APOC ordered him to amend his financial disclosure and file the names of dozens of tenants. His 2026 POFD reported more than $1M in rental income with tenants listed only by first name and last initial (July 27). APOC staff issued a deficiency notice July 21 and found the later list did not substantially comply (AS 39.50.030). Commissioners voted 4–1 to recommend he not be certified. The lieutenant governor disqualified him Aug. 31 and reversed herself Sept. 4.
legal.status: APOC recommendation stands (not withdrawn as of Sept. 5 reporting); certified to the ballot Sept. 4, 2026 by the lieutenant governor; no court ruling

record_extra.t: He gave his campaign $300,000 in cash after the July 17 deadline ($260,000 on Aug. 3 and $40,000 more), plus more than $3,400 in plane tickets. AS 15.13.078 caps a candidate's self-funding at $5,000 after that date, so his gifts were more than 60 times the cap. His running mate and her husband gave $100,000 on July 28; the Beacon says that also exceeded the limit. His campaign calls the limit unconstitutional; no court has ruled.
record_extra.status: As of Aug. 17, 2026 APOC's director knew of no complaint; no later APOC action found

recordx.apoc: notices — Sept. 2025 order to amend; July 21, 2026 notice of deficiency; Aug. 2026 4–1 recommendation against certification. No fine found.

research_notes: RUNNING MATE: final ticket is Taylor/Candice English. Juneau Independent reports the Division of Elections list updated after 11 p.m. Sept. 4. Wikipedia's article still says English named Jodi Taylor; that was true only Aug. 31–Sept. 4. A human should confirm against the Division of Elections' certified candidate list. MONEY: APOC was unreachable (proxy refusal; WebFetch permission not granted). Figures come from Wikipedia's APOC table (Feb. 1), ADN/APM (July) and the Beacon (Aug. 17). The $600,000 self-funding total is Wikipedia's figure and matches Beacon reporting. No corporate or business-PAC money was documented in the sources opened, so money_flags is {}. That is not a verified clean result, and checklist.money_history stays 'news'. Whether Taylor or English refunded the post-deadline money, or APOC opened a case, was not found. 2016 Assembly-race finances were not found. LEGAL: the Department of Law review Dahlstrom relied on is unpublished; a human should check whether APOC later met on it or whether any court challenge was filed after Sept. 5. The 'third longest-serving AG' claim rests only on his own department's release. Wikipedia's note about his wife's disclosures is listed only as context, under his family's shared building.
